chapter_theme: The last quarter of Pattinathar's antadhi on Ekambar of Kanchi: a kovai-like run in which the praise of the god is carried by the land and by love. Kanchi's fields, tanks, groves, bull-embracing greens and seashore are described to a woman, and the lover's departure, the monsoon that is the season of return, the bangles that slip and tighten, and the chariot that arrives are the frame in which Ekambar is named in every stanza. The three closing verses turn to the work itself: service to Ekambar done today and not tomorrow, the hundred verses laid at his feet, and poor words taken as Veda by his true servants.
structure_note: Each verse opens on the last word of the one before (antadhi), and each names Ekambar or Kambar of Kanchi. The sequence moves by landscape: paddy and cane country (929 to 935), the Vishnu shrines within the city (936), the sand-linga legend (938), the monsoon and the lover's chariot (939 to 943), the bull-embracing green (944, 945), the seashore (946 to 950), and the close (951 to 953). The verse keys 929 to 953 are the tool's seq numbers for stanzas 76 to 100 of the work.

929.reading: In the Kanchi of Ekambar whose throat is dark as a rain-cloud, the shouts of ploughmen in the rich mud, of those heaping red paddy like golden hills, and the noise of the cane mills together sound like the roar of the great sea, O woman of fine jewels.
929.nuance: The praise of the god is carried entirely by the plenty of his town: three working noises are heard as one sea. கார்மிக்க கண்டம், the cloud-dark throat, keeps the poison legend in the first line while the rest is harvest.

930.reading: Because her eyes looked out over the long wilderness of the cruel, strong hunters, they have lost their lids, O golden one; because Kambar wrapped himself in the elephant's hide, Uma could not look at him; and because she joined him in the groves of his Kanchi, the cool of the flowering season now excels.
930.nuance: The stanza turns on four ...அமையால் clauses whose subjects must be supplied. I take the lidless eyes as the woman's sleepless watch on the road her lover took, set against Uma who could not bear the sight of Siva in the flayed elephant's skin and yet is joined to him in Kanchi: separation and union laid side by side. The grammar allows other pairings.

931.reading: Lotus tanks where winged bees sing, areca groves whose spathes are full of red-ripe nuts, plantain thickets heavy with sweet fruit: all through the honeyed flower-country of Kanchi of Ekambar of the tawny matted hair it is like this, O woman of fine brow.

932.reading: The dark eyes and red mouths of the fine-browed women go like this, and the blue lily and the red lily that bloom in the pools of the Kanchi country of Ekambar, the land of women with golden brows and eyes, open as if crying out that nothing can match them.
932.nuance: The standard comparison of eyes to lilies is turned round: the flowers of the god's tanks are the ones making the claim (வீறிடும்), and it is unclear whether they vaunt themselves or concede. Either way the land, not the god, is what the stanza praises.

933.reading: Good water, filled deep in close-set moats so that those within are cool, where blade-like vaalai fish and red carp graze; the fair spread of lakes of the Kanchi country where cool blue lilies yield honey, the land of Ekambar, who takes us and gives us no further birth.
933.nuance: கொள்வார் பிறவி கொடாத ஏகம்பர் is the one doctrinal phrase in a landscape stanza: the god who accepts a person does not hand back birth. எங்களை ஆட்கொள்வார் (who takes us as his own) is the Saiva idiom of being ruled.

934.reading: In the cool fields where good water lies like a dark cloud settled in the wide sky, thick with moss and spreading taro, a buffalo with flowing udders eats the flowers, and a bull crocodile that crowds in there fights it, O woman of shining brow: this is the flower-Kanchi of wealthy Kambar.
934.nuance: The fertility is shown as a fight: the field water is deep enough to hold a crocodile. கரா ஒருத்தல் is the male crocodile; பொரப்பார் (will fight) is the verb the stanza ends on.

935.reading: Where the mountain's daughter with bodice-bound breasts could see, Ekambar in his delight set the four pure dharmas; the shrine tower that the gods and vidyadharas worship so that the Goddess rejoices, the hall of charity whose giving never fails, and the ornamented mansions spread wide and rose high.
935.nuance: வெண்ணான்கறம் is read as வெண் நான்கு அறம், the four pure dharmas, perhaps the four kinds of giving; the text has a break (வெண்ணான் கறமும்). அச்சாலை is taken as அறச்சாலை, the charity hall, which the preceding தன்மம் அறா (dharma never ceasing) supports. The stanza praises the built city: tower, alms-house, mansions.

936.reading: Lofty Uragam, Ullagam and the other shrines, and Padagam where Hari dwells in his settled way: the sword-eyed one, the sister-in-law of the other god, stays in that country which the great poets have carried in song, and it is her own house, O woman of ornaments.
936.nuance: ஊரகம் and பாடகம் are names of Vishnu's shrines inside Kanchi, so the stanza folds the Vaishnava city into Ekambar's. மற்றவர் மைத்துனி, the other's sister-in-law, is read as Lakshmi, wife of Vishnu whose sister is Siva's consort, so that Kanchi is her house too. உம்பருருகிடமாம் and தெவ்விரிய are unclear and the sentence does not resolve; the plain sense is that the city holds both gods' houses.

937.reading: Think of the shining of the faultless red that came from the brow-eye of Ekambar who wears the serpent as his jewel, the Lady's own colour, and of the rare trident that none may approach: here is a grove of golden cassia thick with leaves, O golden one, and for us there is no weariness.
937.nuance: The stanza sets the gold of the konrai grove beside the red of the third eye and the Goddess (அருணம் பிராட்டியது). The connections between the lines are loose; I read it as the woman's consolation that in Ekambar's grove, under his signs, there is no tiring, which the next verse carries on with தளரா.

938.reading: Seeing the great untiring flood, Uma ran and embraced him, and the mark of her bangled hands was pressed in: here he worked that trick, in Thiruvekambam of rich groves; having come and bowed here we have gained being alive in this world, O young woman.
938.nuance: This is the founding legend of the shrine: Siva sent the Vegavati in flood to test Kamakshi, who clasped the sand linga she had made, and the bangle marks stayed on it. கிறிபடுத்தார் calls the flood his trick, and the pilgrim's gain is put plainly: உளராவது படைத்தோம், we have obtained being.

939.reading: When the cloud-elephants come in the sky, swinging the lightning as their whip, roaring with thunder from within and streaming with mighty rut, she of the trailing hair, thinking 'who will come after this?', is of the nature of the banner on Ekambar's temple that stood there.
939.nuance: The rains are the season the absent lover promised to return by; the clouds come as rutting elephants and the woman trembles like a flag in the wind. பின்னர் என்பார் இர் என (who will say 'after'?) is hard; the plain sense is that the monsoon has arrived and she waits.

940.reading: Though it is only rain, my eyes are dim, see, cloud; heart, do not fear; if anyone asks who, they will say we are kin; within the long walls of Ekambar in Kanchi, which may be set beside Amaravati itself, if one says 'join', the sword-eyed one stays, for her lover's chariot is coming.
940.nuance: Four என்னிலும் clauses (even if water, even if who, even if equal, even if join) build an address to the heart. The one clear statement is the last: அன்பர் தேர்வரவே, the lover's chariot is coming, which the following stanzas take up. The city is matched with the gods' Amaravati.

941.reading: You who are like Ekambar's Kanchi, where the gods gain boons and good: before your lover's chariot the dark clouds have come, bearing rain-pearls in their waves, with flowers and gold konrai, holding cool kanthal clusters in their hands and golden powder, to scatter them.
941.nuance: The monsoon is made a welcoming party for the returning chariot: clouds carry pearls, gold and scented powder as women do at a homecoming. பரங்கொங்கை தூவன்மின் (scatter them from your high breasts?) is awkward and the subject shifts; the welcome is the sense.

942.reading: Those who worshipped the feet of Kambar who holds the bow in his generous hand and went to conquer their enemies in the face of battle do not think of us; the clouds have darkened and poured like the face of the sea; O woman of fine jewels, with hot sighs we shall swim across the sea of our task face on.
942.nuance: வினைக்கடல் is literally the sea of deeds; here the hero's task of war that keeps him away, which the woman must swim through. வெய்துயிர்ப்பு, hot breath, is the sigh of separation. The variant note printed under 947 (நீந்துமயர்வுயிர்ப்பே) belongs to this stanza's last line.

943.reading: Hearing that the lover who is our life is coming by chariot, our many bangles, which had wilted before, have become like crops that gained a rain-cloud: by the grace of Ekambar, bathed in curd, milk and ghee, they have tightened so that they sink in, O dark peacock.
943.nuance: The slipping bangle, the stock sign of a woman wasting in separation, is reversed: at the news alone the arms fill out and the bangles bite. The god's abhisheka of curd, milk and ghee is the only ritual detail, and it is made the source of the body's recovery.

944.reading: 'Though the seven embrace him of the colour of the dark bull, today alone, gaining the war-bull, they died facing it': so the gods let them go. In the pastures outside Kanchi of Ekambar with the garlanded bull, the young bulls rush at those who daily win golden ornaments on their chests, to be embraced.
944.nuance: This and 945 describe ஏறுதழுவல், the bull-embracing of the herding country, which won a bride. The first two lines are corrupt or elliptical (ஏழ்தழுவினும், அண்டர் போதவிட்டார்); the clear part is the young bulls (மழவிடை) and the youths who embrace them for the ornaments and the girls.

945.reading: Young men whose minds rush to the corner of the spear-like dark eyes of the fine maidens, heedless of the cruelty of the leaping bulls, hold them in Kambar's Kanchi; and in the fields of young jasmine fed by sluices, as fawns and calves bound through every gate, the village green fills and surges like a sea.
945.nuance: The desire that drives the youths at the bulls is said straight: it is the maidens' eyes, not valour. The sea simile that opened the chapter (929) returns for the crowd on the green.

946.reading: O slender girl of the fisherfolk on the sand-hill of thick-scented punnai by the wide sea of Kanchi of Ekambar of cool groves of rising flowers: the two things in your face are not the rich-flowered carp, not the sword, not the spear, not the blue lily, but two sharp arrows of full-blown flowers.
946.nuance: The man's praise of the eyes refuses the four stock comparisons one by one and lands on Kama's flower arrows. The seashore (நெய்தல்) setting continues to 950.

947.reading: If you weigh the old saying that taught 'the face is half and goods are the other half' against the age, what good is it to me? In the Kanchi of high Ekambar, if there is no measure to what is within, O coral-red mouth, let those who have reached us take up this good infatuation.
947.nuance: முகம் பாகம் பண்டமும் பாகம், face half and wealth half, is quoted as an old maxim (மூதுரை) on what wins love, and the stanza seems to set inner measure against it. The third and fourth lines are corrupt (ரகம்பாகவார்லின், நகம்பாற்பொழில்) and the sense cannot be recovered with confidence.

948.reading: They crossed the backwater where sharks that kill in the bewildering dark and striking makara fish ride the tide that sets whirlpools turning, in Kambar's Kanchi by the sea, the Kambar who gives grace to the perplexed; O lord, she cannot bear parting from the embrace of your golden flesh, and she fears the fierceness of the water you come through.
948.nuance: The woman's companion speaks to the hero: the night sea he crosses to visit is the danger, and the god named in passing is the one who gives grace to the confused (துயக்கத்தவர்க்கு அருளா). ஊன் முயக்கம், the embrace of flesh, is unusually direct.

949.reading: The heron feeding where it lies takes no notice, the bees that drink honey hum over the punnai, the tide rushes into the wide sea-mouth: on the shore of pure sand by the sea of Kanchi of Kambar, whom the serpent-bedded one worships, who else knows? Our lord of the shore is false.
949.nuance: The heroine's complaint that the lover has broken faith has only the shore and its creatures for witnesses, and they do not notice. பாயிரை நாகம் கொண்டோன் is read as Vishnu, whose bed is the serpent, worshipping Siva; தூயிரை கானல் as the pure-sanded grove. நந்துறைவர் பொய்யே is the clear line.

950.reading: Kambar of the great grace that comes as truth, who does not let go even the false-hearted and the deceivers: in his Kanchi of fragrant groves, where tame birds and flocks of conches cry, the firm chariot of our lord of the shore, with its garlands crowding and sounding, is drawing near.
950.nuance: The answer to 949: the lover called false arrives, and the god's epithet is chosen to fit, grace that will not abandon even deceivers. The chariot's coming (தேர்வரவு) was promised in 940 and 943.

951.reading: 'We will do it today; how much more good we will do for Thiruvekambar in this; we will do service tomorrow': heart, those who go about in the body thinking so and do not do it, he leaves; those who stand and serve as his slaves without letting a day go, he shows the long path.
951.nuance: The self-address to the heart (நெஞ்சே) is Pattinathar's usual form; here it carries an argument about deferral. நீள்நெறி, the long path, is the way to the god's feet, shown only to those whose service has no gap. The verse does not threaten death; it says the god lets the postponer go.

952.reading: They showed themselves so that the flood of love might pour at their holy feet; those who gathered it worship Ekambar; they bound us who had nothing to them; and gaining love for them we have set down ten tens of songs, praised and worshipped their feet.
952.nuance: The colophon stanza: பதிற்றுப்பத்துப் பாட்டு, a hundred verses, is the antadhi itself, offered at the feet. ஏதுமிலாத எம்மை, us who had nothing, makes the binding the god's act and the poet's love its result, the order Saiva poets keep.

953.reading: Even if one who praises the feet babbles like a madman, the true servants will take even poor-worded compositions that do not shine with wisdom or substance as the shining meaning of the Veda, so long as they say 'praise Ekambar, whose grace keeps the many services from falling into harm'.
953.nuance: The last stanza is the poet's apology and its answer: what makes words scripture is the name they praise and the hearers who serve, not their learning. பித்துப் பிதற்றிலும், though one prattles in madness, is the same self-image Sivavakkiyar uses of his own reciting.

links.note: In both the bangles know before the woman is told: in the Kural they register the lord of the shore's parting before her mind does; here they tighten at the mere news of the chariot, so that the slipping bangle of separation runs in reverse.

Both refuse the deferral of 'today, that day, some day': the Naladiyar puts Death behind the one who asks when, Pattinathar puts the god's leaving behind the one who says 'we will serve tomorrow'. The Naladiyar asks for virtue as far as one can; this verse asks for service without a day's gap.

Two Siddhar prefaces on mad reciting: Sivavakkiyar asks the learned to forgive the errors of one who recites like a madman; Pattinathar says the true servants will take even such babbling as Veda. The apology is the same; Pattinathar supplies the hearers who make the poor words good.

Arunagirinathar confesses he has no great poetry of devotion and that tattvas learned led only to argument; Pattinathar says words that do not shine with wisdom are Veda when they praise Ekambar. Both set the name praised above the poem's learning.

source_issues: The VARIANT_NOTES entry under 947 ('[1] நீந்துமயர்வுயிர்ப்பே - எனவும் பாடம்') is a variant of the last line of 942 (நீந்துதும் வெய்துயிர்ப்பே), not of 947; the note is attached to the wrong unit.
947 lines 3 and 4 are corrupt (ரகம்பாகவார்லினளவில்லையென்னின், நகம்பாற்பொழிற்பெற்ற): no reading of வார்லின் or நகம்பாற் is secure.
935 line 1 has a space inside a word (வெண்ணான் கறமும்); read as one word வெண்ணான்கறமும்.
944 lines 1 and 2 (ஏழ்தழுவினும், அண்டர்போதவிட்டார்) are elliptical or corrupt and the sentence does not resolve.
The text is printed without word division throughout (sandhi-joined), which makes several stanzas (930, 936, 939, 940) hard to parse with confidence.
